---
format:
  revealjs:
    theme:
      - default
      - assets/theme.scss
    width: 1600
    height: 900
    # Figure-heavy science talks that need a text column beside a large figure
    # often read better on a wider canvas. To use ~21:9, set:
    #   width: 2100
    # and scale figure base_size / linewidths up to match (see the setup chunk).
    #
    # center: false keeps content top-aligned and pins the grey data-section
    # watermark to the slide bottom edge. For content-light / card decks that
    # leave a lot of empty space below the content, set `center: true` to balance
    # each slide vertically (it uses the whole slide height instead of clustering
    # at the top). Two interactions to know before flipping it: (1) the
    # data-section watermark then sits just beneath the centred content rather
    # than the slide edge, and (2) `.absolute` bleed-figure slides and
    # `.fit-narrow` assume top-aligned slides, so re-render and re-check those.
    center: false
    slide-number: c/t
    hash: true
    menu: true
    progress: true
    controls: true
    transition: fade
    embed-resources: true
execute:
  echo: false
  warning: false
  message: false
params:
  config_file: "presentation.yml"
  project_root: "."
---

```{r}
#| label: setup
#| include: false
# Keep embedded figures light so the self-contained HTML stays small: render
# inline figures at screen (1x) resolution. Pre-optimize any external images
# into an `optimized/` folder before embedding them (see README "File size").
knitr::opts_chunk$set(
  dev = "png",
  dev.args = list(bg = "transparent"),
  dpi = 96,
  fig.retina = 1
)
source("R/presentation_helpers.R")
if (requireNamespace("ggplot2", quietly = TRUE)) {
  ggplot2::theme_set(presentation_theme())
}
cfg <- read_presentation_config(params$config_file, params$project_root)
validate_presentation_inputs(cfg)
summary_object <- load_presentation_summary(cfg)
spict <- if (identical(cfg$data$adapter, "spict")) {
  extract_spict_context(summary_object)
} else {
  NULL
}
```

## Trajectories should carry the argument {data-section="Results"}

:::: {.text-figure}
::: {.text-panel}
- Put the interpretation beside the visual when the audience needs guidance.
- Keep the text short enough that the figure remains the dominant proof object.

::: {.takeaway}
Use `.text-figure` for concise bullets on the left and a figure on the right.
:::
:::

::: {.figure-panel}
```{r}
#| label: plot-spict-trajectories
#| fig-width: 7
#| fig-height: 4.6
#| out-width: 100%
plot_spict_trajectories(spict)
```
:::
::::

::: {.notes}
Charts should be generated from the compact result object. Use the analysis
project for complex plotting functions and call those functions here when
possible.
:::

## Choose a layout by proof object {data-section="Style sampler"}

:::: {.grid-3}
::: {.card}
::: {.card-title}
`.grid-2` / `.grid-3`
:::

Use cards when the proof object is a small set of comparable concepts.
:::

::: {.card}
::: {.card-title}
`.metric-grid`
:::

Use metric cards for repeated indicators with a shared interpretation.
:::

::: {.card}
::: {.card-title}
`.table-slide`
:::

Use narrow tables when exact scenario values matter more than shape.
:::
::::

::: {.takeaway}
Pick the layout from the evidence type first, then write the slide claim.
:::

::: {.notes}
This sampler slide is meant to make the reusable classes visible in the
starter deck. Delete it from project decks after selecting the relevant
patterns.
:::

## Emphasis styles separate caveats from conclusions {data-section="Style sampler"}

::: {.alert-box}
Use `.alert-box` for a caveat, risk, or modelling limitation that should not be
missed.
:::

:::: {.takeaway-grid}
::: {.takeaway-card}
::: {.card-title}
Finding
:::

The evidence supports one clear statement.
:::

::: {.takeaway-card}
::: {.card-title}
Caveat
:::

The result has one important boundary.
:::

::: {.takeaway-card}
::: {.card-title}
Next step
:::

The audience knows what to do with the result.
:::
::::

::: {.deadline}
Use `.deadline` for review dates, decision points, or meeting constraints.
:::

::: {.closing}
Use `.closing` for a short final line.
:::

::: {.notes}
Use emphasis styles sparingly. They are strongest when the rest of the slide is
quiet.
:::

## A wrapped title can sit beside a full-height figure {.fit-narrow data-section="Style sampler"}

::: {.fit-results}
- Put the interpretation in a narrow column on the left.
- Keep bullets brief — the figure is the proof object.
- Subscript reference points with Pandoc inline notation, e.g. B~MSY~ and
  F~MSY~, so they render correctly in both HTML and PDF.

::: {.fragment}
- A `.fragment` appears on the next click.
:::
:::

<!-- Replace with the real figure path. Portrait: height="1000"; landscape
     (add .fit-narrow-tight to the heading): width="950". -->
![](assets/HI_logo_farger_engelsk.png){.absolute top=-150 right=-100 height="1000"}

::: {.notes}
Use `.fit-narrow` (55 % text width) for portrait or square figures and
`.fit-narrow .fit-narrow-tight` (44 %) for wide landscape figures where the
content reaches further left. Place the figure with `.absolute` — e.g.
`top=-150 right=-100 height="1000"` for portrait or
`top=130 right=-100 width="950"` for landscape — so it bleeds past the slide
margins. Put bullets in a `.fit-results` div; strong-tagged keywords pick up
the `--imr-blue` colour automatically. Avoid wrapping `.fit-results` in a
`.columns` grid: the `.absolute` figure floats independently of flow, so no
container is needed on the text side.
:::

## Swap two figures in the same spot {data-section="Style sampler"}

::: {.r-stack}

::: {.fragment .fade-out fragment-index=1}
```{r}
#| label: plot-swap-a
#| fig-width: 11
#| fig-height: 4.6
#| out-width: 100%
plot_spict_trajectories(spict)
```
:::

::: {.fragment .fade-in fragment-index=1}
```{r}
#| label: plot-swap-b
#| fig-width: 11
#| fig-height: 4.6
#| out-width: 100%
plot_spict_trajectories(spict)
```
:::

:::

::: {.small-note}
Stack figures in a `.r-stack` and pair `.fade-out` / `.fade-in` on the same
`fragment-index` to swap one figure for another in place — useful for comparing
two species, scenarios, or model variants without moving the audience's eye.
:::

::: {.notes}
Both panels here draw the same placeholder; in a real deck the two chunks would
plot different objects. Use `.fade-in-then-out` for the middle steps of a longer
sequence so each figure appears, then clears for the next.
:::

## Pace a multi-figure argument {data-section="Style sampler"}

:::: {.columns}

::: {.column width="40%"}
Reveal one figure per click while the bullet beside it says what to look for —
the text accumulates on the left, the figure swaps on the right.

**First** — establish the baseline.

::: {.fragment fragment-index=1}
**Then** — the comparison fades in over it.
:::

::: {.fragment fragment-index=2}
**Finally** — land the figure you want left on screen.
:::
:::

::: {.column width="60%"}
::: {.r-stack}

::: {.fragment .fade-out fragment-index=1}
```{r}
#| label: plot-seq-a
#| fig-width: 8.4
#| fig-height: 5.4
#| out-width: 100%
plot_spict_trajectories(spict)
```
:::

::: {.fragment fragment-index=1 .fade-in-then-out}
```{r}
#| label: plot-seq-b
#| fig-width: 8.4
#| fig-height: 5.4
#| out-width: 100%
plot_spict_trajectories(spict)
```
:::

::: {.fragment fragment-index=2 .fade-in}
```{r}
#| label: plot-seq-c
#| fig-width: 8.4
#| fig-height: 5.4
#| out-width: 100%
plot_spict_trajectories(spict)
```
:::

:::
:::

::::

::: {.small-note}
Sync each left-column `.fragment` and its figure on the same `fragment-index`.
In the `.r-stack`, the first figure is `.fade-out`, middle figures
`.fade-in-then-out`, and the last `.fade-in`. With transparent figure
backgrounds an earlier figure shows through later ones unless it clears itself,
so every step except the last must fade out.
:::

::: {.notes}
All three chunks draw the same placeholder; in a real deck they would plot
different objects (for example capability, then cost, then an effort trade-off).
This is the pattern behind a text-left / figure-right walkthrough. Keep the base
figure legible on its own in case the presenter skips the fragments. Chunk
labels deliberately avoid the `fig-` prefix so Quarto does not add a "Figure 1"
caption.
:::

## Recreate a concept diagram in HTML/CSS {data-section="Style sampler"}

:::: {.text-figure}
::: {.text-panel}
- When a slide needs a simple "central thing surrounded by contributing
  pieces" diagram, **redraw it in HTML/CSS** rather than embedding a bitmap.
- It stays vector-crisp at any size, picks up the deck's fonts and `--imr-*`
  colours, and is trivial to relabel.

::: {.takeaway}
Reach for `.concept-hub` for a hub-and-spoke; reuse `.grid-3` + `.card` for a
flat labelled grid. Keep bitmaps for photos and genuine external figures.
:::
:::

::: {.figure-panel}
<div class="concept-diagram">
<div class="concept-equals">System =</div>
<div class="concept-box">
<span class="concept-box-label">Boundary</span>
<div class="concept-hub-grid">
<div class="concept-sat pos-top">Input A</div>
<div class="concept-sat pos-left">Input B</div>
<div class="concept-hub">Core</div>
<div class="concept-sat pos-right">Input C</div>
<div class="concept-sat pos-bottom">Input D</div>
</div>
</div>
</div>
:::
::::

::: {.notes}
The centre sits in the middle of a 3x3 grid; add only the satellite cells you
need (`pos-top`, `pos-right`, `pos-br`, `pos-bottom`, `pos-bl`, `pos-left`,
`pos-tl`, `pos-tr`). Good for an assessment model and its data inputs, a stock
and its sources, or any agent/harness-style anatomy. This is hand-built markup,
not a generated figure — edit the divs directly.
:::

## Tables can share a slide with a compact figure {data-section="Style sampler"}

```{r}
#| label: table-style-sampler
knitr::kable(
  data.frame(
    Scenario = c("Reference", "Lower catch", "Higher catch"),
    `Catch (t)` = c("TBD", "TBD", "TBD"),
    `Risk` = c("TBD", "TBD", "TBD"),
    check.names = FALSE
  ),
  align = c("l", "r", "r")
)
```

::: {.scenario-figure}
```{r}
#| label: plot-style-sampler
#| fig-width: 12
#| fig-height: 2.7
#| out-width: 100%
old_par <- par(no.readonly = TRUE)
par(mar = c(2.5, 3.2, 0.4, 0.4), mgp = c(1.8, 0.6, 0))
plot(
  1:6,
  c(2.1, 2.4, 2.2, 2.8, 3.0, 3.2),
  type = "b",
  lwd = 3,
  pch = 19,
  col = "#056A89",
  xlab = "Step",
  ylab = "Relative value"
)
par(old_par)
```
:::

::: {.notes}
Use `.scenario-figure` when a narrow table needs a small visual check beneath
it. Keep the figure compact so the table remains readable.
:::

## Compare scenarios in one table {data-section="Results"}

```{r}
#| label: scenario-table
knitr::kable(
  scenario_table(spict),
  align = c("l", "r", "r", "r")
)
```

::: {.takeaway}
State the decision-facing comparison in one sentence.
:::

::: {.notes}
Keep tables narrow enough to read from the back of the room. Put the full
scenario table in an appendix if more columns are needed.
:::

## End with what should stick {data-section="Close"}

:::: {.takeaway-grid}
::: {.takeaway-card}
::: {.card-title}
Finding
:::

State the most important empirical result.
:::

::: {.takeaway-card}
::: {.card-title}
Interpretation
:::

Explain why that result matters.
:::

::: {.takeaway-card}
::: {.card-title}
Next action
:::

Ask for the discussion, decision, or follow-up you need.
:::
::::

::: {.fragment .fade-in .closing-inline}
Thank you — questions and discussion
:::

::: {.notes}
Do not end on a generic thank-you slide. End on the message the audience should
remember. The `.closing-inline` fragment fades in on the presenter's last click,
so the conclusions boxes are the resting state and the sign-off appears only
when the presenter is ready to invite questions.
:::
